text: At small orders (256, 512) A in C is faster than the Python variant B: there $M$ is comparable to $|G|$ (for groups of order 256 with $d=6$ at $n=5$ $M=1554>255$), and Python has a fixed overhead per group. At order 2187 B is 30 times faster than A in C, and hundreds of times faster than numpy.

For the group of order $3^{494}$ the indices $\log_3|\Delta/\Delta^n|=59, 321, 1430$ ($n=2,3,4$) agreed modulo $3^{19}$ and over $\mathbb Z$. On the 394 tested elements (pcgs of layers 2–4) $D_n=\gamma_n$ for $n\le4$, consistent with Passi's theorem ($D_4=\gamma_4$ for odd $p$).

$D_5\cap\Omega_1(\gamma_3\cap M_5)=1$ in all 14 groups, as in theirs.
$D_4\cap\Omega_1(\gamma_3\cap M_4)$ has rank 1 exactly for $2^{84}$, $2^{90}$, $2^{107}$ and is trivial for the rest, as in theirs.

$\alpha=[e_0,e_1]^{32}[e_0,e_2]^{64}[e_1,e_2]^{128}\in D_4$ for $2^{84}$ and $2^{90}$; for $2^{107}$ and two other groups with $\alpha\ne1$, $\alpha\notin D_4$; for the rest $\alpha=1$. All as in theirs.

The exactness certificate ($p^{E-1}A_n^+\subseteq J_n+p^EA_n^+$) passes in all 42 cases. Therefore the memberships modulo $2^{30}$ are exact here, and $D_4(Q)\ne1$ for $2^{84}$, $2^{90}$ and $2^{107}$ is proved by computation, not merely a "candidate modulo $2^{30}$".

Self-contained check in this repository (scripts/example.sh): GAP exports the SmallGroups of orders 64, 81 and 243 itself, and variant A, variant B from permutations and variant B from a presentation are compared with each other. It needs no reference data: 349 groups, 0 differences.

The original screening of the 3-groups of order $3^7$ is no longer needed: all 3-groups of order $\le3^7$ of class 4 are metabelian, and for them $D_5=\gamma_5$ by Gupta–Tahara 1985. For order $3^7$ it has been done anyway: B went through all 1202 candidates in 157 s on three threads, with $D_n=\gamma_n$ for all $n$ everywhere. Variant A in C independently gave the same (4 905 s on three threads): 1 202 groups, 6 010 levels, 0 differences from B. The point of the kernel now is large groups and 3-groups of order $3^8$ and above.

Orders $3^8$, $2^{10}$ and above. Do not export permutations; instead export from GAP/ANUPQ the pc-presentation and only the generators of $K$ (export_pres.g + magnus_pres.py --kernel). The cost per group is building $J_5$ ($M=30..780$ for $d=2..5$, fractions of a second to seconds) plus the export in GAP. The bottleneck is generation and the sieve in GAP, not the lattice. For $d\ge6$ and $n=5$ ($M\ge1554$) A in C over the whole group is better while $|G|\le2^{11}$.

The Rips group ($2^{38}$). B from a presentation fits: the group has class 3, $n=4$ is needed, and $M=\sum_{k<4}d^k\le399$ even for $d=7$. This is the same as what was already computed for $3^{494}$ and for the Rips-type family $2^{40}$–$2^{107}$ (seconds per group). What is missing is a presentation of the Rips group itself: it was not found in open sources; Mikhailov–Passi, LNM 1952, is needed. Searching for the smallest quotients means adding one relation and recomputing $J_4$, also seconds.
Rewriting B in C/FLINT makes sense only together with the switch to standard monomials (§3.6): at the current sizes ($M\le780$) Python is not the bottleneck.

section: 6.3. An estimate for the plateau question of [IMP26, §3.3]: is $w\in D_7$?

text: Dense (as now). One Howell form $M\times M$ in uint32 is 12.5 GB, twice that with the row pool. The operation count is $\sim M^3/3\approx6\cdot10^{13}$ per pass. On one core (~$10^9$ operations/s in our C) that is 15–20 hours. But $J_7$ is generated not by $M$ but by $\sim\sum_r\sum_{t\le6-\operatorname{ord}r}(t+1)6^t$ rows: about $5\cdot10^4$ per relation with a linear part, that is, of the order of $10^6$ rows, and the closure needs several such passes. In total $10^{14}$–$10^{15}$ operations: days on the test machine, and at the limit of its memory (61 GB, shared with CI). Not recommended.
section: 6.3. An estimate for the plateau question of [IMP26, §3.3]: is $w\in D_7$?

text: Standard monomials (§3.6). The number of columns would be of the order of $\log_2|\Delta/\Delta^7|$ plus the monomials with a non-invertible pivot, that is, probably thousands rather than $5.6\cdot10^4$. That is minutes. Measured in §6.4: not so, at least 23 354 columns. It needs an implementation (the nilpotent quotient of an associative algebra over $\mathbb Z/2^E$): a few days of work. The size can be estimated cheaply in advance: compute $\log_2|\Delta/\Delta^n|$ for $n=2..5$ with the current B ($M\le1554$) and extrapolate.
